Surah 88: al-Ghashiyah. It is Meccan according to all scholars, and it has twenty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾

"Hal" here carries the meaning of "qad" (indeed, certainly), as in His words: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time?﴾ [Al-Insan 76:1]. This is the view of Qutrub, meaning: "Indeed, there has come to you, O Muhammad, the report of the Overwhelming," that is, the Resurrection, which overwhelms creation with its terrors and frights. This is the view of most exegetes (mufassirun). Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "al-Ghashiyah" is the Fire, which covers the faces of the disbelievers, and this was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire will cover their faces﴾ [Ibrahim 14:50]. It has also been said that it covers creation. It has also been said that what is meant is the second blast for the Resurrection, because it overwhelms creation. It has also been said that "al-Ghashiyah" refers to the people of the Fire, who cover it and plunge into it. It has also been said that the meaning of "Has there come to you" is: this was not within your knowledge or the knowledge of your people. Ibn Abbas said: it had not come to him before in this detailed form mentioned here. It has also been said that the phrase is in the form of a question addressed to His Messenger, and its meaning is: if the report of the Overwhelming has not come to you, then it has now come to you; this is the meaning of the view of al-Kalbi.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He had not yet received their story, so He informed him about them, and said: ﴿Faces on that Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Humbled﴾." Sufyan said: "That is, abased by punishment." Every person who is humbled and still is khashi' (humble, submissive). It is said: "He was khashi' in his prayer," when he abased himself and lowered his head. And "the voice was khashi'," meaning it became faint. God Most High says: ﴿And the voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:108] [[Verse 108 of Surah Ta-Ha.]]. The word "faces" here means the people who have those faces.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: "Humbled" means in the Fire. The reference is to the faces of all the disbelievers. This was said by Yahya ibn Sallam. It was also said that it refers to the faces of the Jews and the Christians, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Then He said: ﴿Labouring, weary﴾. This refers to the world, because the Hereafter is not a place of work. So the meaning is: faces that labour and toil in the world, and are humbled in the Hereafter. The lexicographers said: It is said of a man who persists in his journey, "qad 'amila ya'malu 'amalan" (he has laboured). It is also said of a cloud when its lightning persists, "qad 'amila ya'malu 'amalan," and "dha sahab 'amil" (a persistent cloud). Al-Hudhali said:

*Until a weak, exhausted lightning, persistent, drove it on;*
*The cattle spent the night thirsty, and the night spent its whole length without sleep.*

[[This is Sa'idah ibn Juwayyah. "Sha'aha" means "drove it." "Kalil" means weak lightning. "Mawhin" means a portion of the night. "Baatat tarabaan" means the thirsty cattle spent the night longing to proceed to the place where the lightning was. "Wa baat al-layl ajma' la yaqarr" means the lightning is described as not sleeping, because it continued from the beginning of the night to its end. (See this line and its discussion in Khizanat al-Adab, the fourth witness after the six hundredth.)]]

*Nasibah* means exhausted (ta'bah). It is said: "nasiba (with kasra) yansabu nasaban" when he became tired, and also "nasban," and "ansabahu ghayruhu" (someone else tired him).

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "They are those who exhausted themselves in the world in disobedience to God, Mighty and Majestic, and in disbelief, such as the idol-worshippers and the disbelieving People of the Book, such as the monks and others. God, may His praise be exalted, will not accept from them anything except what was sincerely for Him."

Sa'id reported from Qatadah, concerning ﴿Labouring, weary﴾, that he said: "They were arrogant in the world toward obedience to God, Mighty and Majestic, so God makes them labour and exhausts them in the Fire, by dragging heavy chains, carrying shackles, and standing barefoot and naked in the open plains, on a day whose length is fifty thousand years."

Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "They did not labour for God in the world, nor did they toil for Him, so He makes them labour and exhausts them in Hell."

Al-Kalbi said: "They are dragged on their faces in the Fire." And from him and others: "They are commanded to climb a mountain of iron in Hell, so they toil in it with the utmost toil, by struggling with the chains and shackles, wading into the Fire as camels wade into mud, climbing an ascent of fire and descending from a slope of it, and other forms of its punishment." This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa and Humayd recited, and 'Ubayd reported from Shibl from Ibn Kathir, (*nasibatan*) with the accusative, as a circumstantial state (*hal*). It was also said that it is accusative for disparagement (*dhamm*). The rest [of the readers] read it in the nominative, as an attribute, or by supposing an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), and so one stops at *khashi'ah*.

Whoever takes the meaning to refer to the Hereafter may make it a predicate following another predicate of *wujuh*, and then one does not stop at *khashi'ah*.

It was also said: *'amilah nasibah* means laboring in the world and exhausted in the Hereafter. On this reading, the meaning may be: faces on that Day, laboring in the world, exhausted in the Hereafter, humbled.

'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: "They worked in the world at sins."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 4:

﴿تَصْلى نَارًا حامِيَةً﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 4]. That is, it will suffer its burning and its heat. "Hamiyah" means intensely hot: it has been kindled and heated for a long duration. From the same root comes "hamiya al-nahar" (with a kasra on the ha'), and "hamiya al-tannur hamyan" in both cases, meaning its heat intensified. Al-Kisa'i reported: "ishtadda hamy al-shams" and "ishtadda hamwuha" (the heat of the sun intensified), with the same meaning.

Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read ﴿تُصْلَى﴾ with a damma on the ta'. The rest read it with a fatha. It is also read ﴿تُصَلَّى﴾ with tashdid. The discussion of these readings has already been given under "Idha al-sama' infatarat" [al-Inshiqaq: 1].

Al-Mawardi: If it is asked, what is the meaning of describing it as "hamiyah," when it can only be hot, and that is its least state? So what is the point of emphasizing it with this deficient attribute? It is said: there are four views on what is meant by "hamiyah" here.

First: it means that it is perpetually hot, unlike the fire of this world whose heat ceases when it is extinguished.

Second: "hamiyah" means that it is a protected preserve (himan) against committing what is forbidden and violating what is sacred, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed every king has a preserve, and the preserve of God is His prohibitions. Whoever grazes around the preserve is about to fall into it."

Third: it protects itself from being touched or approached, just as a lion protects its den. Similar is the saying of al-Nabigha:

The wolves attack the one who has no dogs, and they fear the assault of the lion that protects its own.

Fourth: it is hot with anger and rage, as an exaggeration of the intensity of retribution. It does not mean heat of body and essence, as one says: "So-and-so became hot," when he is enraged and angry, intending retribution. Allah the Exalted has made this meaning clear by His saying: ﴿تَكادُ تَمَيَّزُ مِنَ الْغَيْظِ﴾ [al-Mulk: 8], "it almost bursts with rage" [al-Mulk: 8].

Al-Ā'iyah: the one whose heat has reached its limit, from al-Ināʾ (the reaching of a boiling point, i.e. intense heat) [[Āniyah: extremely intense in heat, from anā yaʾnī, like ramā yarmī; it is not from al-Ināʾ, the verbal noun of ānā with another meaning. Al-Ṭabarī said in his tafsir of the verse: "They are given to drink from a spring whose heat has reached its limit, having attained its utmost intensity."]], in the sense of delay. From this comes the expression "ānayta wa-ādhayta" [[That is, in the hadith about the Friday prayer, in which he said to a man who came on Friday stepping over the necks of the people: "You have delayed and you have harmed." The meaning of "ānayta" is: you delayed coming and were slow. And "ādhayta" means: you harmed the people by your stepping over them.]]. And ānāhu yuʾnīhi ināʾan means: he made him hot, detained him, and made him slow. From this comes the verse ﴿They will go around between it and a scalding hot water﴾ [[Verse 44 of Surat al-Rahman.]] [al-Rahman: 44]. In the tafsirs, "from a spring āniyah" means that its heat has reached its limit; so if a single drop of it fell upon the mountains of the world, they would melt. Al-Hasan said: "āniyah" means its heat has reached its utmost; Hell has been kindled beneath it since it was created, so they are driven to it as thirsty herds. It is narrated from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "It has reached its ultimate point, and the time of its drinking has come."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They shall have no food but from *dari'*﴾, that is, for the people of the Fire. Since He mentioned their drink, He mentioned their food.

'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: *al-Dari'* (ضَرِيع) is a thorny plant that lies flat on the ground. Quraysh call it *al-Shibriq* (الشِّبْرِق) while it is fresh, and when it dries it becomes *al-Dari'*. No animal or beast comes near it or grazes on it. It is a deadly poison and the most foul and repulsive of foods. The majority of exegetes hold this view. However, al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "It is something the sea casts up, called *al-Dari'*, a food for livestock and not for people. When camels fall into it they are not satisfied, and they perish from emaciation." The sound view, however, is that of the majority: that it is a plant. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*"He grazed on the lush al-Shibriq until it withered,*
*and when it turned into dari', the she-asses (al-naha'if) left it."*[[We have not found this verse in the Diwan of Abu Dhu'ayb.]]

[[In some copies of the original: "the she-asses (al-nahaʾis) left it." Al-nahaʾis is the plural of al-nahuṣ (with a fatha on the nun), meaning a wild she-ass that is barren. It is also said: one that is pregnant with a foal. It is also said: one that has no milk.]]

And al-Hudhali [[He is Qays ibn 'Ayzara, as in Lisan (al-'Arab).]], describing camels and their poor pasture, said:

*"They were confined in the crushed dari',*
*so all of them were hunched, with bleeding forelegs, and barren."*[[Hazm al-dari': what has been broken off of it. Al-hadba' (the hunched one): a she-camel whose hip bones have become prominent and whose back bone is visible. Al-harud: one that hardly yields milk.]]

Al-Khalil said: *al-Dari'* is a green plant with a foul smell, which the sea casts up. Al-Walibi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "It is a tree of fire; and if it existed in this world, it would burn the earth and everything on it." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It is stones," and 'Ikrimah said the same. The most apparent view is that it is a thorny tree, in keeping with what exists in this world.

And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "*Al-Dari'* is something that grows in the Fire, resembling thorns, more bitter than aloes, more foul-smelling than carrion, and hotter than fire. Allah named it *dari'*."

Khalid ibn Ziyad said: I heard al-Mutawakkil ibn Hamdan being asked about this verse, ﴿They shall have no food but from dari'﴾. He said: "It has reached me that *al-Dari'* is a tree of the Fire of Hell, whose fruit is pus and blood, more bitter than aloes. That is their food."

Al-Hasan said: "It is part of the punishment that Allah has concealed." Ibn Kaysan said: "It is a food over which they humble themselves and grovel, and from which they implore Allah, the Exalted, seeking deliverance from it. It is named thus because the one who eats it entreats to be spared from it, because of its repulsiveness and harshness."

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "It may be derived from *al-dari'*, meaning the humbled, that is, one who has humility (*dara'a*), meaning whoever drinks it is humbled and afflicted with humility."

And also from al-Hasan: "It is the *zaqqum*." It has also been said: "It is a valley in Hell." And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted has said in another place: ﴿So he has no friend here today, nor any food except from *ghislin*﴾ [al-Haqqah: 35–36]. Here He said: ﴿except from *dari'*﴾, and this is other than *ghislin*. The way to reconcile this is that the Fire has levels (*darakat*). Some of them have *zaqqum* as their food, some have *ghislin*, some have *dari'* as their food, some have *hamim* as their drink, and some have *sadid* as their drink.

Al-Kalbi said: "*Al-Dari'* is in one level, in which there is nothing else, and *al-zaqqum* is in another level." It is also possible that the two verses refer to two states, as He said: ﴿They will go around between it and scalding, boiling water﴾ [al-Rahman: 44].

Al-Qutabi said: "It is also possible that *al-Dari'* and the tree of *zaqqum* are two plants of fire, or of a substance that fire does not consume. Likewise the chains of the Fire, its shackles, its scorpions and its serpents. If they were as we know them, they would not remain in the Fire." He said: "Allah has only pointed us to what is unseen with Him by means of what is seen by us. So the names agree in indication, while the meanings differ. Likewise is what is in Paradise of its trees and its couches."

Al-Qushayri said: "A more fitting view than that of al-Qutabi is to say: the One who keeps the disbelievers in the Fire so that the punishment may continue upon them, keeps the plant and the tree of *zaqqum* in the Fire so that the disbelievers may be punished by them." Some of them claimed that *al-Dari'* itself does not grow in the Fire, nor do they eat it. So *al-Dari'* is of the food of livestock, not of the food of people. When camels fall into it they are not satisfied, and they perish from emaciation. He meant that these people feed on what does not satisfy them, and He presented *al-Dari'* as an example for them: that they are punished by hunger, just as one is punished whose food is *al-Dari'*.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: "This is a feeble view from its proponents and a base interpretation. It seems to imply that they were bewildered about the power of Allah, the Exalted. The One who caused this *dari'* to grow in this earth is able to make it grow in the blaze of the Fire. He placed for us in this world fire within green trees: the fire does not burn the tree, and the moisture of the water within the tree does not extinguish the fire. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree, and then from it you kindle﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]. As was said when the verse was revealed, ﴿and We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾ [al-Isra': 97], they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how will they walk upon their faces?' He said: 'The One who made them walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces.' Only one weak of heart is bewildered by such a thing. Did He not inform us that whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins [al-Nisa': 56], and He said: ﴿Their garments will be of pitch﴾ [Ibrahim: 50], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 12], meaning fetters; and ﴿a blazing Fire, and food that chokes﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 13]. It was said: that is, thorny. The punishment is thus varied upon them through these things."

It means the ḍarīʿ (a thorny plant) does not fatten the one who eats it. And how could one who eats thorns grow fat!

The exegetes said: When this verse was revealed, the polytheists said, "Indeed our camels grow fat on the ḍarīʿ." So the verse was revealed: "It neither fattens nor satisfies hunger." But they were lying, for camels only graze on it while it is fresh; when it dries out, they do not eat it.

It was also said that its matter was confused for them, so they assumed it was like other beneficial plants, because the word mudāraʿa means resemblance. Then they found that it neither fattens nor satisfies hunger. [[In some copies: (لا يشبه).]]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 8–10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be joyful﴾, meaning possessing bliss (dhat ni'mah). They are the faces of the believers, who are made joyful by what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and their righteous deeds. ﴿For their striving﴾, meaning for their deeds which they performed in this world. ﴿Satisfied in the Hereafter﴾, when they are given Paradise in return for their deeds. Its figurative sense is: satisfied with the reward of their striving. In it there is an implied wa (waw, "and"). The meaning is: "And faces that Day," for the separation between them and the faces mentioned earlier. And "faces" is an expression for the selves (al-anfus).

﴿In a lofty Garden﴾, meaning elevated, because it is above the heavens, as has been mentioned previously. It was also said: lofty in rank, because in it is what the souls desire and the eyes find delight in. ﴿They will abide therein forever.﴾

They are the faces of the believers, who are made joyful by what they witnessed of the outcome of their affair and their righteous deeds. ﴿For their striving﴾, meaning for their deeds which they performed in this world. ﴿Satisfied in the Hereafter﴾, when they are given Paradise in return for their deeds. Its figurative sense is: satisfied with the reward of their striving. In it there is an implied wa (waw, "and"). The meaning is: "And faces that Day," for the separation between them and the faces mentioned earlier. And "faces" is an expression for the selves (al-anfus).

﴿In a lofty Garden﴾, meaning elevated, because it is above the heavens, as has been mentioned previously. It was also said: lofty in rank, because in it is what the souls desire and the eyes find delight in. ﴿They will abide therein forever.﴾

Allah's statement: ﴿Thou shalt not hear therein any idle talk﴾ (88:11). That is, speech that is worthless and unacceptable. He said "lāghiyah," and "al-laghw," "al-laghā," and "al-lāghiyah" have one meaning. [The poet] said:

"From idle talk and obscene speech"

[The line is preceded by:]

"And many a host of pilgrims, dense..."

Its speaker is Ru'bah; Ibn Barri attributed it to al-'Ajjaj.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: that is, you will not hear therein a single word of idle talk. As for what is meant by it, there are six views:

First: it means lies, slander, and disbelief in Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: no falsehood and no sin. This was said by Qatadah.

Third: that it is cursing (shatm). This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: disobedience (ma'siyah). This was said by al-Hasan.

Fifth: no one swearing an oath by a lie will be heard therein. This was said by al-Farra'. Al-Kalbi said: no one will be heard in Paradise swearing an oath, whether a truthful oath or a false one.

Sixth: no word of idle talk will be heard in their speech, because the people of Paradise speak only with wisdom and with praise of Allah for the everlasting bounty He has provided them. This too was said by al-Farra'. And this is the best of these views, because it encompasses all that has been mentioned.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "lā yusma'u" with a yā' and without naming the subject. Nafi' likewise, except that he used a tā' with a damma, because "lāghiyah" is a feminine noun, so he made the verb feminine to match it. Whoever read with a yā' did so because the prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa'l-majrūr) intervened between the noun and the verb. The rest read with a tā' with a fatha, "lāghiyatan," explicitly attributing the action to the faces (al-wujūh), meaning: "let no faces hear idle talk therein."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 88, verse 12–16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾, meaning with flowing water and various delicious drinks on the surface of the earth, without a trench. It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Insan that therein are springs [[See vol. 19, pp. 124, 104]]. So "ʿaynun" (a spring) here is in the sense of "ʿuyun" (springs). And Allah knows best.

(Therein are raised couches) meaning elevated. It is related that their height was as far as between the heaven and the earth, so that the friend of Allah may see his dominion around him.

(And cups set in place) meaning ewers and vessels. The ibrik (ewer) is that which has a handle and a spout. The kub (cup) is a vessel that has neither a handle nor a spout. This has already been mentioned in Surat al-Zukhruf [[See vol. 16, p. 113]] and elsewhere. And (cushions lined up) meaning pillows, the singular being numruqah. Lined up meaning one placed beside the other. The poet said:

And indeed we pass the cup among our drinking companions,
And between Abi Qabus, above the cushions.

And another said:

Elders and youths, fair of face,
Upon couches and cushions lined up.

In al-Sihah: al-numruq and al-numruqah: a small cushion. Likewise al-nimriqah (with kasra) is a dialectal form related by Yaʿqub. And they sometimes call the saddle-cloth that is placed atop the riding saddle a numruqah, according to Abu ʿUbayd.

(And carpets spread out): Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-zarabi are rugs (busut). Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-zarabi are saddle-cloths (tanafis) that have a thin nap; its singular is zarbiyyah. Al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said likewise. And al-mabthuthah means spread out; so said Qatadah. It was said: some of them placed above others; so said ʿIkrimah. It was said: many; so said al-Farra'. It was said: scattered throughout the gatherings; so said al-Qutabi. I say: this is more correct, that they are many and scattered. From the same root is His saying: ﴿And He scattered therein every kind of creature﴾ [[Verse 164, Surat al-Baqarah.]] [al-Baqarah: 164]. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ahmad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, who said: Husayn ibn ʿArafah narrated to us, who said: ʿAmmar ibn Muhammad narrated to us, who said: I prayed behind Mansur ibn al-Muʿtamir, and he recited: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the Overwhelming?﴾, and he recited in it: ﴿And carpets spread out﴾, ﴿reclining therein, luxuriating﴾.

Scholars of tafsir said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the matter of the people of the two abodes, the disbelievers marveled at this, so they denied and rejected it. Then Allah reminded them of His craftsmanship and His power, and that He is capable of everything, as He created the animals, the sky and the earth.

Then He mentioned the camel first, because it is abundant among the Arabs, and they had not seen the elephant. So He drew their attention to a great creature of His creation, which He has made subservient to a small one: one leads it, makes it kneel, makes it rise, and carries on it heavy loads while it is kneeling, and it rises with the weight of its heavy load. No other animal does this. Thus He showed them a great creature of His creation made subservient to a small creature of His creation, guiding them by this to His oneness and the greatness of His power.

It is related from some sages that he was told about the camel and its wondrous creation, while he had grown up in a land with no camels. He reflected and then said: "It is likely that it has long necks." And when He willed that they should be ships of the desert, He made them patient in bearing thirst, to the extent that their thirst may extend to ten days or more, and He made them graze on everything that grows in the wastelands and deserts, which other livestock do not graze on.

It was also said: When He mentioned the raised couches, they said: "How shall we climb them?" So Allah revealed this verse and showed that camels kneel until a load is placed on them and then they rise; likewise those couches lower themselves and then rise. This was said by Qatadah, Muqatil and others.

It was said: "The camels" here means the great clusters of clouds; this was said by al-Mubarrad. Al-Tha'labi said: "It was said that 'the camels' here means the clouds, but I have found no basis for this in the books of the imams." I (al-Qurtubi) say: al-Asma'i, Abu Sa'id Abd al-Malik ibn Qarib, mentioned that Abu 'Amr said: whoever reads it as "afala yanzuruna ila al-ibli kayfa khuliqat" with light (takhfif) intends by it the camel, because it is one of the four-legged animals that kneel so that loads may be placed upon it, whereas other four-legged animals are not loaded except while standing. And whoever reads it with emphasis (tathqil), saying "al-ibil," intends by it the clouds that carry water and rain.

Al-Mawardi said: Regarding "al-ibil" there are two views. The first, which is the more apparent and well known, is that they are camels of the livestock. The second is that they are clouds. If the intended meaning is clouds, then it is because of the signs in them that point to His power and the general benefits for all His creation. If the intended meaning is camels of the livestock, then it is because the camel combines more benefits than any other animal, for its kinds are four: milk-giving, riding, eating, and carrying loads. The camel combines these four qualities, so the blessing in it is more general and the manifestation of power in it is more complete.

Al-Hasan said: Allah singled it out for mention only because it eats date-pits and fodder and produces milk. Al-Hasan was also asked about it, and they said: "The elephant is greater in wonder." He said: "The Arabs are far removed from knowledge of the elephant; moreover, it is a pig whose meat is not eaten, whose back is not ridden, and whose milk is not milked."

Shurayh used to say: "Come with us to al-Kunasah [[al-Kunasah: the market of Kufa, to which camels bearing merchandise come or from which they depart; it is like al-Mirbad for Basra.]] so that we may look at the camels and see how they were created."

"Al-ibl" has no singular from its own form, and it is feminine, because collective nouns that have no singular of their own form, when they refer to non-human beings, take the feminine necessarily. When you diminutive them, the ta' marbutah is added, so you say: Ubaylah and Ghunaymah, and similar forms. Sometimes they say for the camels "ibl," with the ba' vowelless for lightness, and its plural is "aabal."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And at the sky, how it was raised?﴾ That is, it was raised above the earth without pillars. It was also said: "It was raised, so nothing can reach it."

(And at the mountains, how they were set firm.) That is, how they were set firmly upon the earth so that they do not move. When the earth was spread out, it shook, so He anchored it with the mountains, as He said: ﴿And We placed firm mountains upon the earth lest it shake with them﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya, verse 31].

(And at the earth, how it was spread out.) That is, it was extended and stretched. Anas said: "I prayed behind ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and he recited (kayfa khuliqat) and (rufiʿat) and (nusibat) and (suṭiḥat), with a ḍammah on the tā's, attributing the verb to Allah the Exalted." Muḥammad ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and Abū al-ʿĀliyah also recited this way, and the object is omitted, meaning "He created it," and likewise for the rest. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Ḥaywah and Abū Rajāʾ recited (suṭṭiḥat) with a shaddah on the ṭāʾ and a sukūn on the tā'. The majority recited it the same way, except that they read the ṭāʾ without a shaddah.

He mentioned the camel first in the remembrance. Had He mentioned something else first, it would have been permissible. Al-Qushayrī said: "This is not one of the matters in which a particular wisdom is sought." It has also been said: the camel is closest to people in the case of the Arabs, because it is abundant among them, and they are among the people most knowledgeable about it. Also, the benefits of the camel are greater than those of other animals: its flesh is eaten, its milk is drunk, it is suitable for carrying loads and riding, for covering long distances on it, for enduring thirst, for needing little fodder, and for carrying heavy loads, and it constitutes the greater part of the wealth of the Arabs. They used to travel on camels alone, distant from people. Whoever is in this state reflects on what is before him: he may look at his mount, then raise his gaze to the sky, and then to the earth. So they were commanded to contemplate these things, for they are the clearest proof of the Maker, the Chooser, the Powerful.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 88, verses 21–26:

Allah's words: "So remind (fa-dhakkir)", meaning: admonish them, O Muhammad, and warn them. "You are only a reminder (mudhakkir)", meaning: an admonisher.

"You are not over them a controller (bi-musaytir)", meaning: not one empowered over them so that you would kill them. Then it was abrogated (nasakhathha) by the verse of the sword. Harun al-A'war recited "bi-musaytir" with a fatha on the ta' (bi-musaytir). The word "al-musaytirun" appears in the verse "(Surah al-Tur, 37) [al-Tur: 37]," and this is the dialect of Tamim.
